design_detail: Record-linkage study of two Norwegian sources of drug deaths, notifications 2007–2009. Source 1: the Cause of Death Registry (CDR): physicians' death certificates coded in ICD-10, with drug-induced deaths selected by the EMCDDA definition (underlying cause F11–F12, F14–F16 or F19; or X41, X44 or Y11 with T43.6 as the first contributing cause; or X42, X44, Y12 or Y14 with any of T40.0–T40.9 as the first contributing cause; or the suicide codes X61 or X64 with T43.6, or X62 or X64 with T40.0–T40.9). Source 2: the police registry of drug deaths: unnatural deaths that physicians must notify to the police, investigated by local police, reported to the National Criminal Investigation Service and selected by local and central police as drug overdoses or drug deaths, without ICD codes and with drug information in one non-standardized spreadsheet column. Persons were matched on the national personal identification number, then manually (same date of death, sex, age, concordant cause and place of death) against CDR deaths with an F, X or Y underlying cause; 11 were matched manually. Four groups (police registry without a CDR match; police registry with a CDR cause outside the definition; both; CDR/EMCDDA only) were compared with chi-square tests, and CDR-only against both with logistic regression. Single author.
can_establish: How far Norway's Cause of Death Registry (under the EMCDDA definition) and the police registry counted the same people as drug deaths in 2007–2009, and how the people counted by only one source differed in age, sex, certified cause, first-listed drug, autopsy and place of death.
cannot_establish: Which source was right about any discordant death (no reference standard or case review); why deaths were missing from either source (the reasons offered are not measured); how many drug deaths both sources missed; or whether deaths in the 'morphine/codeine' group came from medicines rather than heroin certified as morphine.

sample.recruitment: Registers: notifications for 2007–2009 from the Norwegian Cause of Death Registry (EMCDDA definition) and from the police registry of drug deaths (pp. 75–76).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: CDR: Norwegian residents only, deaths meeting the EMCDDA definition, counted by year of death (delayed certificates are added later and are said to be few). Police registry: all unnatural deaths regardless of residency, selected by the police as drug deaths (p. 75).
sample.demographics: 929 persons: 725 men (78%) and 204 women (22%). Mean age 42.7 years (95% CI 41.4 to 44.0) in the CDR/EMCDDA-only group against 35.3 (34.3 to 36.2) in both registries (p. 76; Table 1, p. 77).
sample.attrition: Not applicable (records). 33 police-registry persons could not be matched: 39% were not Norwegian citizens and the rest had missing or erroneous ID numbers.
sample.selection_effects: Two registers with different rules (residency, definition, who reports and selects), so non-overlap mixes differences in definition, reporting and investigation. Table 1 takes cause, drug and place of death from the CDR for matched persons; the police registry's own drug information is used only for the 33 unmatched (Table 1, footnotes a–c). National police figures were published only until 2009.

exposure.measurement: How a death entered each count, and who decided. CDR: physicians must issue a death certificate for the deaths they encounter; the CDR codes it in ICD-10, applying ICD-10 rules that can adjust the certificate's information, and the EMCDDA selection uses only the underlying and the first contributing cause (pp. 75, 77–78). Police registry: physicians must notify the police of unnatural deaths, including use or suspected use of narcotics; the police decide whether an autopsy is performed, generally when the cause is uncertain or unknown and the death sudden and unexpected, with no obligation when narcotics are suspected as the cause; local police investigate (previous knowledge of the person, evidence at the scene, witnesses, health and emergency personnel), add autopsy information if it is available before submission, and local and central police select the deaths they label drug overdoses or drug deaths (p. 75). What was tested: autopsy in 715 of 822 CDR/EMCDDA deaths (Table 2), 431 of 455 in both registries and 284 of 367 CDR/EMCDDA-only (editors' sums from Table 1); toxicology coverage is not reported.
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Not reported; route of use is not recorded in either source as analysed.
exposure.polysubstance: One drug per person is analysed: the first contributing T-code in the CDR, or the first-mentioned drug in the police registry. The Discussion cites a Nordic study giving a median of 4–5 drugs per fatal poisoning, excluding alcohol (p. 78).

comparison.controls: The two registries compared with each other; neither is a reference standard, and the author states that neither should be considered the correct figure for drug deaths in Norway (p. 78).
comparison.matching: Not applicable (linkage on the personal identification number).
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Not applicable (counts of deaths). Prescriptions, route of use, treatment and service contact were not available.

outcomes.instruments: Group membership (Fig. 2, p. 76); characteristics by group with chi-square tests (Table 1, p. 77); adjusted odds ratios of being in the CDR/EMCDDA count only rather than in both, for 822 CDR/EMCDDA deaths (Table 2, p. 78); a first comparison of all CDR/EMCDDA deaths with all police-registry deaths as differences in proportions with confidence intervals (p. 76); yearly counts 1996–2009 from a published source (Fig. 1, p. 75).
outcomes.validity_norms: Neither registry is validated against toxicology or case review.
outcomes.operationalization: 'Drug-induced death': the EMCDDA code selection in the CDR. 'Drug death': the police selection. 'Type of drug': the first contributing T-code (CDR) or first-mentioned drug (police). 'Cause of death' groups: dependence, overdose, suicide, other (CDR underlying cause).
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: None: 11 chi-square tests in Table 1, 6 differences in the first comparison and one multivariable model; most p-values are below 0.001.

analysis.effect_sizes: Overlap: 455 of 929 (49%) in both; 367 (40%) CDR/EMCDDA only; 74 (8%) in the police registry with a CDR cause outside the definition; 33 (4%) in the police registry without a CDR match. Editors' calculation: the police registry lacked 367 of 822 CDR/EMCDDA deaths (44.6%), and the CDR/EMCDDA count lacked 107 of 562 police-registry deaths (19.0%). CDR/EMCDDA-only against both: mean age 42.7 (41.4 to 44.0) against 35.3 (34.3 to 36.2); dependence or suicide as underlying cause 33% against 8%; heroin as first contributing drug 24% against 67%; among women, morphine/codeine 47% against 16%. Adjusted odds ratios of being CDR/EMCDDA-only rather than in both (n = 822): women 1.05 (0.68 to 1.61); under 25 0.35 (0.20 to 0.64), 25–39 0.65 (0.45 to 0.92), 60 and over 3.77 (0.99 to 14.3), against 40–59; suicide 1.9 (1.09 to 3.36) and dependence/other 10.6 (3.09 to 36.4), against overdose; morphine/codeine 6.89 (4.35 to 10.9), methadone 3.69 (2.29 to 5.96), synthetic opioids 4.63 (2.06 to 10.4), stimulants 2.36 (1.16 to 4.76), none or other codes 1.84 (0.71 to 4.73), against heroin; no autopsy 2.66 (1.42 to 4.98); hospital or other institution 2.61 (1.49 to 4.56), other place 1.02 (0.67 to 1.54), place not reported 0.55 (0.33 to 0.91), against home. First comparison, described as all CDR/EMCDDA against all police-registry deaths (the values reproduce with the 529 police-registry persons who have a CDR record; reporting issue 4), differences in proportion: male 0.014 (−0.014 to 0.041); dying at home 0.016 (−0.032 to 0.064); under 40 years 0.107 (printed CI 0.107 to 0.141); overdose 0.054 (0.032 to 0.076); heroin 0.109 (0.085 to 0.134); autopsy 0.051 (0.031 to 0.071).
analysis.covariates: Table 2 model: sex, age group, cause of death, type of drug, autopsy and place of death together; interaction terms with sex were tested and none was significant.
analysis.preregistration_detail: No protocol is mentioned; permissions came from the Regional Committees for Medical and Health Research Ethics, the Office of the Public Prosecutor and the CDR in Statistics Norway (p. 76).
analysis.selective_reporting: The source of the police group's values in the first comparison is not stated; they reproduce from Table 1 only if the police group is the 529 police-registry persons with a CDR record, compared on CDR variables (editors' calculation; reporting issue 4).
analysis.power: Not reported; intervals are wide for small groups (30 persons aged 60 and over; 32 with synthetic opioids).

interpretation_gap.results_show: Of 929 people registered as drug deaths in Norway in 2007–2009 by the CDR under the EMCDDA definition (822) or by the police (562), 455 (49%) were in both; 367 (40%) were only in the CDR/EMCDDA count; 74 (8%) were in the police registry and in the CDR but with a cause outside the EMCDDA definition; 33 (4%) police-registry deaths had no CDR record (39% not Norwegian citizens, the rest with missing or erroneous ID numbers). Deaths found only in the CDR/EMCDDA count were older and more often certified as dependence or suicide, with morphine/codeine, methadone or synthetic opioids rather than heroin as the first contributing drug, without autopsy, and in hospitals or other institutions.
interpretation_gap.claimed: (1) The conclusion that prevention measures based on the two sources will differ is supported descriptively. (2) The Discussion's reasons for non-overlap (health personnel not reporting deaths to the police; the police not treating every drug death as suspicious; ICD-10 coding of certificates; more complete autopsy information in the CDR; different publication times) are proposed, not measured (pp. 76–78). (3) The morphine/codeine group is read as deaths from pharmaceuticals, especially among women and disability pensioners (p. 78); the paper does not consider that some deaths certified as morphine may be heroin deaths, the misclassification measured in Victoria by Stam et al. (2019; card sc_stam_2019), and it has no data on prescriptions, routes of use or service contact, on which its prevention remarks (switching from injecting to smoking, take-home naloxone, substitution treatment) depend. (4) The statement that the CDR figures are more complete rests on size and overlap, not on a reference standard; the author also says neither source gives the correct figure. (5) Figure 1's trends are called surprisingly similar up to 2009, although the police count is lower in every year and the gap is wider from 2002 onwards (read from the figure; values not printed).

timeline.event: Edland-Gryt (ed.), Alcohol and Drugs in Norway 2012 (Table 5.4): yearly CDR/EMCDDA and police counts for 1996–2009, the source of Fig. 1; the police count is lower in every year.
Simonsen et al. (as cited, p. 78): fatal poisonings among people who use drugs in the Nordic countries in 2012, with a median of 4–5 drugs per case excluding alcohol; not read for this card.

Amundsen (as cited, p. 78): people who died of drug-related causes by the CDR/EMCDDA definition fell into three equal-sized socioeconomic clusters (very low socioeconomic status, disability pensioners, people on the edge of the workforce); not read for this card.

Stam et al. (Victoria, 2012–2013; card sc_stam_2019): deaths certified as morphine, or in generic multi-drug terms, were a main source of heroin deaths missing from national coded counts, which bears on how this paper's morphine/codeine group can be read.

Fugelstad et al. (Sweden): mortality-register statistics, including the EUDA specification, compared with toxicology data; by its title, statistics based on death certificates miss one-third of cases. Listed for this page; not read for this card.

replication.where_it_stands: The author knew of no similar linkage of a cause-of-death register with a police register. Other comparisons of register counts with fuller case information, in Victoria (card sc_stam_2019) and New Mexico (card sc_landen_2003), likewise find substantial disagreement in both directions, driven by definitions, certificate wording and reporting routes. A Swedish comparison of register data with toxicology (Fugelstad et al., 2020) is listed for this page but has not been read here.

funding.declared_conflicts: There are no conflicts of interest (as printed, p. 79).
funding.affiliations_note: Single author at the Norwegian Institute of Public Health; most of the work was done at the Norwegian Institute of Alcohol and Drug Research, which merged with the Institute on 1 January 2016 (pp. 74, 78–79). Recorded as a flag for closer reading.

what_would_settle_it: Linking both registries to forensic toxicology results for every death, with a blinded review of discordant cases (CDR/EMCDDA-only and police-only) by forensic pathologists, would show which deaths each source misses or wrongly includes and why; the same review of deaths certified as morphine or codeine would show how many were heroin deaths.

domains.domain: 1. Sample frame appropriate to the target population
domains.note: The national CDR (all certified deaths of residents) and the national police registry are the frames for drug deaths in Norway; the CDR excludes non-residents.
All notifications for 2007–2009 in both registers; no sampling.
929 persons; some groups are small (33 unmatched; 30 aged 60 and over in Table 2).

domains.domain: 4. Study subjects and setting described in detail
domains.note: The groups are described by sex, age, cause, drug, autopsy and place of death, and both registration processes are described.

domains.domain: 5. Data analysis with sufficient coverage of the identified sample
domains.note: All 929 persons appear in Table 1; the 33 unmatched have police data only, explained by non-citizenship or ID problems.

domains.domain: 6. Valid methods for identifying the condition
domains.note: The CDR selection uses an explicit code list but only the first contributing cause; the police selection is unstandardized and undocumented; neither is checked against toxicology or case review.

domains.domain: 7. Condition measured in a standard, reliable way across participants
domains.note: Linkage on the personal identification number is reliable; police drug information is free text; the source of the police group's variables in the first comparison is not stated (they reproduce from Table 1 with the 529 police-registry persons who have a CDR record).

Chi-square tests and logistic regression suit the question, but the first comparison treats the two overlapping registries as independent samples, one interval has its lower limit equal to the estimate, one p-value does not match its chi-square, and Table 1 has sum errors.

domains.domain: 9. Adequate response rate, or low rate managed

risk_of_bias.reasoning: JBI-prevalence fits a linkage of two death registers (round brief, record-linkage studies). The overlap counts rest on reliable identifier linkage of complete national registers and are internally consistent; what the non-overlap means cannot be separated into definition, reporting and investigation, because the police selection is undocumented and no discordant case was reviewed, and the comparative statistics have several reporting errors. Citable for: in Norway in 2007–2009 only 49% of 929 people counted as drug deaths by either source were counted by both; 367 deaths in the CDR/EMCDDA count (44.6% of it) were absent from the police registry; these were older, more often certified as dependence or suicide, more often had opioids other than heroin as the first contributing drug, less often autopsied and more often died in institutions. Not citable for: which source is correct, why deaths were missing, or that the morphine/codeine deaths were from medicines.

key_findings.finding: The two sources held 1,384 registrations, 822 in the CDR under the EMCDDA definition and 562 in the police registry, covering 929 people; 11 were matched manually after matching on the personal identification number.

Only 455 of the 929 (49%) were in both the CDR/EMCDDA count and the police registry; 367 (40%) were in the CDR/EMCDDA count but not in the police registry; 74 (8%) were in the police registry with a CDR record whose cause of death was outside the EMCDDA definition, 23% of them with an unspecified cause of death linked to a disease; 33 (4%) were in the police registry with no CDR record, 39% of them not Norwegian citizens and the rest with missing or erroneous ID numbers.

Compared with people in both registries, those only in the CDR/EMCDDA count were older (mean age 42.7 years, 95% CI 41.4 to 44.0, against 35.3, 34.3 to 36.2), more often had dependence or suicide as the cause of death (33% against 8%) and less often heroin as the drug (24% against 67%); among women, morphine or codeine was the drug in 47% against 16%. Autopsy was more common in both registries, and death in a hospital or other institution more common in the CDR/EMCDDA-only group.

Adjusted odds ratios (logistic regression, n = 822) of being in the CDR/EMCDDA count only rather than in both: women 1.05 (0.68–1.61), p = 0.827; under 25 years 0.35 (0.20–0.64) and 25–39 years 0.65 (0.45–0.92) against 40–59; 60 and over 3.77 (0.99–14.3), p = 0.051; suicide 1.9 (1.09–3.36) and dependence/other 10.6 (3.09–36.4) against overdose; morphine/codeine 6.89 (4.35–10.9), methadone 3.69 (2.29–5.96), synthetic opioids 4.63 (2.06–10.4), stimulants 2.36 (1.16–4.76) and none or other codes 1.84 (0.71–4.73) against heroin; no autopsy 2.66 (1.42–4.98); hospital or other institution 2.61 (1.49–4.56) and place not reported 0.55 (0.33–0.91) against home.

Table 1 by group (no CDR match, police with CDR cause outside the definition, both, CDR/EMCDDA only): men 29, 47, 378 and 271; women 4, 27, 77 and 96. Among men, heroin was the first-listed drug for 15, 4, 260 and 75, and morphine/codeine for 0, 1, 33 and 69; among women, heroin for 0, 2, 44 and 13, and morphine/codeine for 0, 0, 12 and 45. Autopsy among men 0, 38 (81%), 357 (94%) and 205 (76%); among women 0, 18 (67%), 74 (96%) and 79 (82%).
key_findings.note: For the no-match group, drug information is the police registry's first-mentioned drug; for the others, the CDR's first contributing T-code (footnote b). The 0 autopsies printed for the 33 unmatched police-registry deaths most likely reflect the absence of CDR data for them (the autopsy rows appear to come from the CDR) rather than the absence of autopsy: the Methods list police autopsy results as a variable, but Table 1 does not say which source its autopsy rows use (editors' inference).

key_findings.finding: First comparison of all CDR/EMCDDA deaths with all police-registry deaths (differences in proportion, with CI): male 0.014 (−0.014 to 0.041) and dying at home 0.016 (−0.032 to 0.064), not significant; under 40 years 0.107 (0.107–0.141); overdose 0.054 (0.032–0.076); heroin as cause 0.109 (0.085–0.134); autopsy 0.051 (0.031–0.071).
key_findings.note: The minus signs are visible on the rendered page but missing from the PDF's text layer. The interval for under 40 years is printed with its lower limit equal to the estimate (reporting issue 3). The differences reproduce from Table 1 with the 529 police-registry persons who have a CDR record, not with all 562 police-registry deaths (reporting issue 4).

key_findings.finding: Who decides in Norway: physicians must issue death certificates, which go to the CDR (ICD-10 since 1996); physicians must also notify the police of unnatural deaths, including use or suspected use of narcotics; the police decide whether an autopsy is performed, generally when the cause is uncertain or unknown and the death sudden and unexpected, but with no obligation to order one when narcotics are suspected; local police investigate and report to the National Criminal Investigation Service, which published national figures until 2009.

How the police registry is built: information from previous knowledge of the deceased, evidence found or seized at the scene and witnesses, with autopsy information added if completed and available before submission; drug information is not standardized (one spreadsheet column); local and central police select deaths, including narcotics in the EMCDDA definition, and label them drug overdoses or drug deaths; no ICD codes. The CDR registered only Norwegian residents; the police registered all unnatural deaths regardless of residency.

The EMCDDA definition applied to the CDR counts only the underlying cause and the first contributing cause of death, in fixed pairs: dependence codes F11–F12, F14–F16 or F19 as the underlying cause; accidental poisoning X41, X44 or Y11 as the underlying cause with T43.6 as the first contributing cause, or X42, X44, Y12 or Y14 with any of T40.0–T40.9; self-poisoning X61 or X64 with T43.6, or X62 or X64 with any of T40.0–T40.9. X41 is never paired with a T40 code, nor X42 with T43.6.
key_findings.locator: Methods and materials, 3rd paragraph and list

key_findings.finding: Reasons the author gives for the non-overlap, not tested: health personnel fail to report some deaths to the police, and the police do not treat every drug-related death as suspicious (offered for the 367 not in the police registry); a drug may be mentioned on the certificate but not given as the underlying cause, and ICD-10 rules are applied at registration; autopsy reports may be more complete for the CDR's decisions; and, in 2007–2009, the police published in the first half of the year and the CDR late in the second half (offered for the 74).

The author states that neither source should be considered the correct figure for drug deaths in Norway: the costs and regulations of autopsy mean some drug deaths go undetected, so the figures may be too low, and a definition counting all deaths with illegal drugs or medicines with abuse potential as a contributing cause would give higher figures. The author also judges the CDR figures more complete.

Yearly counts 1996–2009 (Fig. 1, from Edland-Gryt 2012): the police count of drug deaths was lower than the CDR/EMCDDA count in every year; the author calls the two trends surprisingly similar up to 2009. Values are not printed and were not extracted.
key_findings.locator: Methods and materials, 2nd paragraph; Fig. 1; Discussion, 5th paragraph

reporting_issues.issue: Table 1, women in both registries: overdose is printed as 68 (86%), but 86% of 77 is 66, the women's overdose total (128) requires 66, and with 68 the column sums to 79, not 77; Table 2's 666 overdose deaths also imply 66 (editors' calculation).
reporting_issues.consequence: Read 66; the percentages and totals are right.

reporting_issues.issue: Table 1: the men's age block for the no-match group is headed 33 (100), but there are 29 men in that group and the age rows sum to 29; in the men's type-of-drug block the Total column differs from the sum of the groups in four rows (editors' sums: heroin 354 against 353 printed, morphine/codeine 103 against 107, synthetic opioids 19 against 20, none or other codes 123 against 119).
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; use the group columns. The men's morphine/codeine total is 103, not 107.

reporting_issues.issue: In the first comparison the proportion under 40 years is printed as 0.107 with CI 0.107 to 0.141, the lower limit equal to the estimate; the other intervals there are symmetric around their estimates (editors' calculation: a symmetric interval would put this lower limit near 0.073).
reporting_issues.consequence: The interval cannot be cited as printed; the difference itself is probably right.

reporting_issues.issue: The first comparison is described as all CDR/EMCDDA deaths against all police-registry deaths and is analysed as two independent samples, although 455 people are in both; the source of the police group's values is not stated. Its differences reproduce from Table 1 if the police group is the 529 police-registry persons with a CDR record (74 + 455), compared on CDR variables with the 822 CDR/EMCDDA deaths: male 425/529 against 649/822 (0.014); dying at home 238/529 against 383/822 (0.016, police lower); under 40 years 341/529 against 442/822 (0.107); heroin 310/529 against 392/822 (0.109); autopsy 487/529 against 715/822 (0.051); overdose 456/529 against 666/822 (0.052, printed 0.054; 0.053 to 0.056 with the misprinted 68 of reporting issue 1) (editors' calculation). The printed intervals are narrower than independent-samples intervals for these counts (autopsy: 0.018 to 0.083, editors' calculation, against 0.031 to 0.071 printed).
reporting_issues.consequence: The comparison appears to use the police-registry persons who have a CDR record, which the paper does not say; because the two groups share 455 people its intervals are not valid as printed. Cite the group comparisons in Tables 1 and 2, or the first comparison's differences without their intervals, with this caveat.

reporting_issues.issue: For place of death among women, chi-square 23.8 with 6 degrees of freedom is printed with p = 0.006; the other printed p-values match their statistics (editors' calculation: for these values p is about 0.0006).
